newsitem.title: Rwanda: Zairean rebels said to have seized town, airstrip.
newsitem.headline: Zairean rebels said to have seized town, airstrip.

text.p: Zairean rebels have seized the southeastern town of Kalemie and its airstrip, military sources in the region said on Monday while a senior Zairean government official in Kinshasa said they were going to bring in troops from African allies to help fight the rebels.

"Togo, Morocco and Chad are all prepared to send troops along with materials. Egypt has offered materials mostly to equip the infantry," the defence ministry official, who asked not to be identified, told Reuters. He could not give a definite date for the arrival of the foreign troops.

The military sources, monitoring Africa's latest war in eastern Zaire, told Reuters the rebels' entry into Kalemie, a key port on Lake Tanganyika and birthplace of rebel leader Laurent Kabila, had sent residents into festive mood.
They said Kalemie fell late on Sunday after heavy fighting between government troops and rebels of Kabila's Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (ADFL).
"I can tell you with certainty that Kalemie has fallen to rebel forces. The latest information is that even the airstrip has been overrun," a military source in central Africa said.
There was no independent confirmation available of the fall of Kalemie. In Kinshasa, a senior Zairean defence ministry official said the army was battling to hold on to the town.

"Since last night there has been heavy fighting in the northern part of Kalemie," he told Reuters. "The FAZ (Zaire army) controls it but reinforcements are having to be sent in from the military base at Kamina."
He added that rebels had taken the town of Watsa, in Upper Zaire far to the north of Kalemie, but that foreign mercenaries backing the army were defending the airport there.
Kalemie, a trading town at the head of a railway link to the mineral-rich Shaba provincial capital of Lubumbashi, is the birthplace and hometown of rebel leader Kabila.
The Lumbumbshi railway links Zaire's southeast to the copperbelt region of Zambia and South Africa.

"Government troops have been pushed out of town, which is now calm apart from celebrating residents, and the only fighting we know of are mop-up operations outside Kalemie," a military source in the region said.
The source said his information was government troops had been pushed up to 20 km (12 miles) outside Kalemie on the route south to the lake port town of Moba, the next rebel target.
"In Kalemie we only hear of jubilant residents. People there are celebrating the arrival of the rebel force," he said.
The source said residents had lined the streets of Kalemie on Monday to welcome the rebel force Zaire says is backed by troops from Rwanda and Uganda. Both nations deny involvement.
He added that rebels were surrounding the town of Lubutu, the last town on the road northwest to the northeastern regional capital Kisangani, a centre for a government counter-offensive.
"They are certainly besieging Lubutu. They are reinforcing around the town but they (rebels) appear to have made no major move on the town as yet," the source said.
EU Commissioner for Humanitarian Affairs Emma Bonino visited refugees on Sunday at Tingi Tingi, seven km (four miles) east of Lubutu, and described their conditions as beneath human dignity.
The rebels responded to the government offensive last month by opening new fronts to the south and west from the long, thin strip of eastern territory they seized in October and November.
Zairean troops and some 300 foreign mercenaries gathered in Kisangani for their counter-offensive ordered by President Mobutu Sese Seko, who left France on Monday for Morocco to meet King Hassan.
